notes:
I've gathered substantial material from multiple sources. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes, drawing from what each source actually says.

---

# Exodus 14 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — "Then the LORD said to Moses"

- **Gill:** The Lord spoke to Moses "out of the pillar of the cloud in which he went before them," either at Etham or shortly after departing from there, just before they turned aside as now directed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

---

## v. 2 — "Tell the Israelites to turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth…"

- **Ellicott:** The Israelites had been marching south-east and had reached the edge of the desert near the head of the Bitter Lakes. Continuing would have taken them safely out of Egypt. The command to "turn" was a deflection to the right (south-east to south), keeping them within Egypt's borders. Some (Kalisch, Rosenmüller) thought "turn" meant "return/retrace steps," but Ellicott says this is wrong — they had not reached the sea before. To reach the Red Sea, they must deflect south. Pi-hahiroth, Migdol, and Baal-zephon cannot be certainly identified; they were small Egyptian towns near the head of the Gulf of Suez. The accumulation of names "indicates an accurate acquaintance with Egyptian topography, such as no Israelite but one who had accompanied the expedition is likely to have possessed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Gill:** "Turn" means turn off the road they were in, not return to Egypt. Gill cites the traveler Dr. Shaw, who identified a valley called "Tiah beni Israel" (road of the Israelites) leading to the Red Sea. Pi-hahiroth may mean "mouth of the rocks" (two rocks with a valley between), or "a place where grew great plenty of grass and herbs." Baal-zephon the Targums take as an idol — the only one left of the idols of Egypt. Gill inclines to think Migdol and Baal-zephon were fortified places guarding the straits to the Red Sea. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God "set an ambush for Pharaoh." The command to camp by the sea was strategically vulnerable — humanly speaking it made no sense. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## v. 3 — "For Pharaoh will say… 'They are wandering the land in confusion; the wilderness has boxed them in.'"

- **Ellicott:** "Entangled" means literally confused, perplexed (cf. Esther 3:15). Pharaoh saw Israel had placed the Bitter Lakes on their left and were marching south, soon to have the Red Sea on one side and the desert (Jebel Atakah) on the other. He would conclude they were ignorant of geography and had lost their way. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This was exactly what God wanted Pharaoh to believe. God told Moses to lead Israel in a way that looked confused, "because God would gain honor over Pharaoh through it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Spurgeon (sermon):** Israel was shut in on either side by craggy mountains, with the Red Sea ahead. God led them into this apparent death-trap deliberately. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israel-at-the-red-sea)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** God changed Israel's direction from south-east to due south. Had they continued, they would have come to arid, treeless wastes with no food or water. Southward lay better-watered territory, though still within Egypt's borders. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-14.html)

---

## v. 4 — "And I will harden Pharaoh's heart… I will gain honor by means of Pharaoh… the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD."

- **Gill:** God would harden Pharaoh's heart "once more, as he had often done," so that Pharaoh would pursue them all the way into the sea. God would be "honoured upon Pharaoh, and upon all his host; in his wisdom, faithfulness, power, and justice, by the destruction of them." The Egyptians who remained in Egypt (not those drowned) would know Jehovah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God was not finished answering Pharaoh's question from Exodus 5:2: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey His voice?" The Red Sea miracle spoke to Egypt as much as to Israel. Ephesians 3:10-11 shows God uses His victories in believers' lives to teach angelic beings — it is testimony to "unseen adversaries." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## v. 5 — "When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds…"

- **Ellicott:** The change of heart began as soon as Israel left. The emigration "left Eastern Egypt a solitude, suspended all the royal works that were in progress, threw the whole course of commerce and business into disorder." Neither king nor people had understood what losing 600,000 labourers — some highly skilled — would mean. When Israel was gone, they realized it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The question "What have we done?" was strange — there were at least ten good reasons (the plagues) to let Israel go. This demonstrates "how we are often quick to forget what God has done." Perhaps Pharaoh thought the plagues were the limit of God's power. There is a spiritual analogy: "We sometimes think that Satan will let us go easily… yet just like Pharaoh after Israel, Satan pursues us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Gill:** The Targums and Jarchi suggest military officers (or spies) who had gone out with Israel reported back when the Israelites did not return after three days. On the fourth day they told Pharaoh; on the fifth and sixth he pursued; on the seventh night he entered the sea, and on the morning of the seventh day Israel sang the song. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 6–7 — "So Pharaoh prepared his chariot… 600 of the best chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt…"

- **Ellicott:** Egyptian monarchs of the Rameside period almost always led their armies in a two-horse chariot with a single charioteer. "Made ready" means ordered to be made ready. The 600 chosen chariots likely constituted a division of the royal guard, always at the king's disposal. "All the chariots of Egypt" must not be pressed literally — it means all available in Lower Egypt (Memphis, Heliopolis, Bubastis, Pithom, Pelusium, etc.), probably several hundreds. The largest attested chariot force is 3,940 gathered by confederates against an Assyrian king. Rameses II faced 2,500 in his Hittite campaign. So 600 is "quite within the limits of probability." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Gill:** These were "choice" or "chosen" chariots — the best war chariots, perhaps with iron scythes. To the question of where horses came from after the hail destroyed livestock (Exodus 9:25), Gill answers: only those in the field were killed, not stabled horses. The Targum of Jonathan says these belonged to servants of Pharaoh who "feared the word of the Lord" and brought their cattle home (Exodus 9:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

---

## v. 8 — "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh… the Israelites were marching out defiantly."

- **Ellicott:** "With an high hand" means confidently, boldly, perhaps somewhat proudly — they had brought the Egyptians to entreat them to leave (Exodus 12:33). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The Hebrew phrase *ruwn yad* includes the idea of rebellion against authority (cf. 1 Kings 11:26-27). This rebelliousness was good when directed against Pharaoh, but bad when directed against the LORD. "The trouble with most rebels is that they rebel against the wrong things." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## v. 9 — "The Egyptians… overtook them as they camped by the sea near Pi-hahiroth, opposite Baal-zephon."

- **Ellicott:** "All the horses and chariots of Pharaoh" — literally "all the chariot-horses." Ellicott argues that "horsemen" (cavalry) are indeed intended, though Egyptian battle art rarely shows them. Diodorus Siculus gives Sesostris 24,000 cavalry; Shishak invaded with 60,000; Herodotus mentions Amasis leading an army on horseback. Egyptian monuments mention cavalry. Ellicott surmises artistic conventions prevented depicting cavalry. Pharaoh's host had all three arms: cavalry, infantry, and chariots. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 10–12 — Israel's fear and complaint: "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt…?"

- **Ellicott:** The fear was legitimate. The 600,000 Israelite men were mostly unarmed, untrained, and "ignorant of warfare." Egypt's force, though smaller, was composed of trained, well-armed soldiers. "Above a million Persian soldiers were defeated and slaughtered like sheep by 47,000 Graeco-Macedonians at Arbela." Israel's cry to the LORD was right: "There is no help like that of Jehovah." The sarcasm about "no graves in Egypt" was "bitter irony," but probably without conscious reference to Egypt as "a land of tombs." Their reproach that they had told Moses this in Egypt was "unjust and undeserved" — they had mostly acquiesced in his leadership. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Israel did the right thing in crying out to the LORD, but their words to Moses "showed little faith and a loss of confidence in God." Kaiser notes the satirical tone: "Egypt specialized in graves and had about three-fourths of its land area available for grave sites." Israel was "not yet a week out of Egypt and they already distorted the past, thinking that it was better for them in Egypt than it really was." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Spurgeon:** The three difficulties Israel faced are typical of the new believer: (1) a great trial sent by God (the Red Sea), (2) old sins pursuing (the Egyptians), and (3) a faint heart (their panic). "The pangs after we come out of Egypt are at times even more painful than those we feel in the house of bondage." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israel-at-the-red-sea)

---

## vv. 13–14 — "Do not be afraid. Stand firm… The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still."

- **Ellicott:** There are times when all our strength must be "in quietness and confidence" (Isaiah 30:15). Normally God "helps those who help themselves," but there are occasions "when we can do nothing — when all must be left to Him" (cf. 2 Chronicles 20:17). Moses probably did not yet know *how* God would deliver, but was confident He would. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Moses had no idea how God would help; "all he knew was God certainly would." When our only help is God, we are more likely to trust Him. "Stand still": despair casts you down, fear tells you to retreat, impatience tells you to do something now, presumption tells you to jump into the Red Sea before it is parted. "The LORD will fight for you" — Cole notes that "salvation" here is used in its literal sense of saving life or victory in war, though the OT later develops a more spiritual sense (Psalm 51:12). The phrase "you shall see them no more forever" implies more than the present moment — Moses "perhaps spoke in terms of eternity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** Moses knew Pharaoh's pursuit was part of Jehovah's design. "His was the confidence of faith." "Stand still, and see" — there are times when we must wait upon the Lord to show His direction. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-14.html)

- **F.B. Meyer:** "It is hard to stand still when the situation becomes acute. If you don't know what to do, stand still until you do; it is God's business to direct and defend the believing soul." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/exodus-14.html)

- **Spurgeon:** Israel had three helps matching their three trials: (1) Providence (the pillar), (2) covenant assurance (God had brought them there and was bound in honour to bring them out), and (3) a man — Moses, who typifies Jesus. "Thy greatest refuge, O child of God! in all thy trials, is in a man: not in Moses, but in Jesus." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israel-at-the-red-sea)

---

## vv. 15–16 — "Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to go forward. Lift up your staff… divide the sea."

- **Ellicott:** Moses had been crying to Jehovah (though he only tells us indirectly). God's answer: "it was not a time to cry, but to act." Israel must strike tents at once. Moses must go to the sea's edge with his rod, stretch it out, and await the division. The exact mode of destruction was not yet revealed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Before the people, Moses was full of faith; before God, he cried out in desperate prayer. This was right — Moses needed to show confidence publicly. But God said: "There is a time to pray, and a time to act. It can actually be against God's will to stop doing and to only pray." Spurgeon is quoted: "There is a time for praying, but there is also a time for holy activity." Trapp adds: "We must not only crave God's help, but be forward in the course whereby to make way for God's help." Clarke notes: "Neither Moses nor his rod could be any effective instrument in a work which could be accomplished only by the omnipotence of God; but it was necessary that he should appear in it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "There is a time for prayer; and there is a time for action. In this instance, Moses had come to the time of action." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-14.html)

- **Gaebelein:** After speaking words of faith (vv. 13–14), Moses began to pray. The Lord's question "Wherefore criest thou unto Me?" is followed by the command to go forward — "the command to go forward, to stretch out the rod over the sea." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 17–18 — "I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians… The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD."

- **Gill:** God would harden the Egyptians' hearts so they would have "no sense of danger, and be fearless of it, incautious and thoughtless, hurried on with wrath and fury, malice and revenge." The destruction was "in just retaliation for the many innocent infants that had been drowned by them in the river Nile." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The goal is that Egypt would finally know who the LORD is — God was still answering Pharaoh's question from Exodus 5:2. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## vv. 19–20 — The angel of God and the pillar of cloud move behind Israel; darkness to Egypt, light to Israel.

- **Ellicott:** The "Jehovah" of Exodus 13:21 becomes "the angel of God" here, just as "the angel of Jehovah" in the burning bush (Exodus 3:2) becomes "God" (v. 4) and "Jehovah" (v. 7). The angel is distinguished from the cloud and directs its movements. The double purpose: (1) to trouble the Egyptians with "cloud and darkness," and (2) to cheer Israel with abundant light for their arrangements. The translators' additions "to them" and "to these" bring out the true sense, confirmed by the Targums and Syriac version. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Gill:** The Jews say this angel was Michael, the great prince. Gill agrees if Michael is understood as the uncreated angel, the eternal Word, the Son of God — "for certainly this Angel of the Lord is the same with Jehovah." The Targum of Jonathan adds the cloud received arrows and stones cast by the Egyptians. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The same pillar that blocked the Egyptians also protected their lives temporarily — "if they had submitted to the LORD who blocked their way, they would have been spared." Kaiser: "Thus the double nature of the glory of God in salvation and judgment, which later appears so frequently in Scripture, could not have been more graphically depicted." The word of God, the gospel, and even Jesus Himself have a dark side to sinners. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Spurgeon (sermon "The Glory in the Rear"):** The glory of God is our rear-guard (Isaiah 52:12; 58:8). What was before them now protects behind them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 21–22 — Moses stretches out his hand; the LORD drives back the sea by a strong east wind; Israel crosses on dry ground, walls of water on right and left.

- **Ellicott:** The "strong east wind" could blow from any point between NE and SE. Ellicott proposes a natural mechanism: if the Bitter Lakes were joined to the Red Sea by a narrow shallow channel, a south-east wind could drive the Bitter Lakes water northward while the ebb tide pulled the Red Sea water southward, leaving a portion of the channel dry. An Egyptian tradition (Artapanus, cited by Eusebius) "distinctly stated that 'Moses waited for the ebb tide in order to lead the Israelites across.'" Ellicott leaves open whether God used purely natural forces or supernaturally increased them. "The waters were divided" — the Bitter Lakes separated from the Red Sea. As for "walls of water," Ellicott says "any protection is in Scripture called 'a wall'" (1 Samuel 25:16; Proverbs 18:11; Isaiah 26:1). The poetical language of Psalm 78:13 and Exodus 15:8 about waters "standing on an heap" should not be pressed into "a narrow literalism" turning poetry into prose. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The Hebrew *yam suph* means "Reed Sea." Scholars debate whether the crossing was at the Bitter Lakes/Lake Timsah region or at the Gulf of Aqaba (Nuweiba Beach, Straits of Tiran, etc.). Guzik cites a 1992 *Los Angeles Times* article on computer modeling showing that "a moderate wind blowing constantly for about 10 hours could have caused the sea to recede about a mile and the water level to drop 10 feet." But Guzik is careful: "Even if God used natural phenomenon, it was still a great miracle." He quotes Adam Clarke's strong reaction against rationalizing the miracle away: "Poor infidelity! how miserable and despicable are thy shifts!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Gaebelein:** "Higher criticism has tried to explain this miracle as a natural occurrence, but they overlooked the fact that on the right and on their left the waters were a wall." It was a grave into which Israel passed by faith (Hebrews 11:29). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-14.html)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist:** "The text implies that Israel marched by night, through the sea: The path was completely dry; not one Israeli arrived on the other side with muddied feet!" Israel was "baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:2), in acknowledgment of Moses' authority — a type of baptism into Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 23–25 — Egyptians pursue into the sea; at morning watch the LORD throws them into confusion; chariot wheels wobble.

- **Ellicott:** All the Israelites having entered the sea-bed, the pillar of cloud withdrew after them. The Egyptians, hearing the sound of departure, began to advance. "They can scarcely have entered on the bed of the sea without knowing it." They probably assumed the sea-bed would stay dry long enough for chariots to cross — perhaps less than a mile, ten minutes. But then the LORD "looked unto the host of the Egyptians through the pillar… and troubled" them — "by some terrible manifestation of His presence and of His anger." A panic seized them. Some stopped, some fled, some persevered. Ellicott notes two textual options for the wheels: the Hebrew text says wheels parted from axles; the LXX and Samaritan Pentateuch say wheels "became entangled" as if sinking in soft ooze. The Egyptians recognized supernatural intervention: "the LORD is fighting for them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** God "miraculously worked on the side of Israel against the Egyptians." He troubled them until Israel had fully crossed, then allowed the pursuit to resume. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## vv. 26–28 — Moses stretches out his hand; the sea returns; the entire army of Pharaoh drowned; not one survived.

- **Ellicott:** The command was probably given "as soon as the Israelites were safe across." At daybreak (about 5 a.m.), the light showed the Egyptians their danger — "the white-crested waves were seen advancing on either side." They raced against the waters but in vain: "Their chariot wheels clogged, themselves and their horses encumbered with heavy armour, they made but slow way over the soft and slimy ground." The flooding overwhelmed them. On whether Pharaoh himself drowned: Ellicott argues it is unlikely — Menephthah (the probable Pharaoh) reigned at least eight years and records that on one great occasion he declined to lead troops personally, claiming the god Phthah forbade him to leave Memphis (Brugsch, *History of Egypt*). He probably stayed with the infantry reserve. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Gill:** The destruction was "in just retaliation for the many innocent infants that had been drowned by them in the river Nile." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-14.html)

---

## vv. 29–31 — Israel walked on dry ground; Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore; the people feared the LORD and believed.

- **Ellicott:** "Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore" — this detail "indicates the pen of an eyewitness." The destruction of the chariot force and cavalry "secured the retreat of Israel" and saved them from further molestation. "The spirit of the nation was effectually broken for the time." The king despaired of fighting a supernaturally protected foe; the army had lost its elite chariot corps. "The episode in the life of the nation begun by the descent of Jacob into Egypt now terminated, and a fresh beginning was made." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This confirmed that deliverance from Egypt was "real and complete. An oppressed people are slow to believe they are free while their tyrants still live. God wanted Israel to know that their oppressors were dead." Israel "feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses" — this was the intended outcome: reverent trust in God and confidence in His chosen leader. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

- **Grant's Commentary (Brethren):** Verse 29 emphasizes dry land — "in type believers have 'died with Christ.' They have passed through death without being touched by it." Reaching the other side "pictures the believer having been raised with Christ (Colossians 3:1), now safe on the other side of death." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-14.html)

- **Gaebelein:** The Red Sea is "a type of the death of Christ. Deliverance from sin by being dead with Christ is the aspect which the Red Sea passage illustrates… the truth so fully brought out in Romans 6:7 and 8. When Israel had passed through the Red Sea and reached the other side, we have a type of resurrection." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-14.html)

---

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
- **Typological reading:** The Red Sea crossing is the believer's "baptism into Christ" — a thorough dedication/consecration following conversion. Trials come soon after conversion to "baptize" the believer into wholehearted service. "It is not when we are first converted that we so fully dedicate ourselves to God, as afterwards, when some great Red sea rolls before us." The three helps (Providence, covenant, and the Man — Christ) match the three trials (providential difficulty, pursuing sins, faint heart). (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israel-at-the-red-sea)

### Baptist (Garner-Howes)
- **Baptism typology:** Crossing the Red Sea is "a type of baptism. The believer is baptized 'unto Christ,' in acknowledgment of His authority, and as a sign of his deliverance from sin's bondage." Emphasis on the dry path and complete deliverance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-14.html)

### Reformed / Brethren (Grant, Gaebelein)
- **Death-and-resurrection typology:** The Red Sea passage illustrates being "dead with Christ and risen with Him." Israel passing through the sea = the believer passing through death without being touched by it. The Egyptians dead on the shore = "our old enemy is gone, and we can look upon our enemies as dead." (Grant: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/exodus-14.html; Gaebelein: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/exodus-14.html)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- **Applied to personal spiritual victory:** Emphasis on God as "Defender," the need to stop praying and start acting when God directs, and the testimony to "unseen adversaries" (Ephesians 3:10-11). The parting of the sea is seen as both naturally plausible (wind-setdown research) and unmistakably miraculous. The believer must sometimes "stand still" and let God fight. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)

---

## Other Views

*Note: I was unable to complete searches for Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), and modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) due to search tool limits. These would need to be researched in a separate session.*

### Older "Rationalist" Tendency (noted and resisted by Ellicott and Clarke)
- **Ellicott** presents a natural-mechanism hypothesis (wind + tide in the Bitter Lakes channel) but leaves it open whether God supernaturally intensified the forces. He also resists the literal "walls of water" reading, treating it as poetic metaphor for protection. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-14.html)
- **Adam Clarke** (quoted in Enduring Word) vehemently opposed naturalistic explanations: "To hear those who profess to believe this to be a Divine revelation endeavouring to prove that the passage of the Red Sea had nothing miraculous in it, is really intolerable. Such a mode of interpretation requires a miracle to make itself credible." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-14/)
